Why Inovexa

## Built for the Modern Enterprise

Finance, HR, stock and sales share the same data, so nobody re-types numbers from one tool into another.

### Lightning-Fast Performance

Screens open in under a second across all 11 modules, and the app stays usable on slower mobile connections.

### Enterprise-Grade Security

Data is encrypted at rest and in transit. Role-based permissions control who sees what, and the audit log records every change.

### Modular & Built to Scale

Start with the modules you need today and switch on more as you grow, from a 10-person team to a company of thousands, without migrating.

# Tailored for Every Industry

Inovexa ERP adapts to your industry with tailored workflows, local compliance, and modular deployment.

Manufacturing Retail Distribution Healthcare +2 more industries

Industries We Serve

## Workflows built for your sector

Each vertical comes with pre-configured workflows, compliance templates, and KPI dashboards built for how your industry actually works.

### Manufacturing

End-to-end factory management from raw materials to finished goods - with real-time production tracking and quality control.

- Predictive maintenance alerts before a breakdown stops the line
- Plan raw material purchases from real production orders and forecasts
- Full traceability from BOM to delivery with quality checkpoints

[Get a demo](https://inovexa-erp.com/contact.html#form-section)

### Retail

Run your physical stores and e-commerce operations with synchronized inventory, customer data, and omni-channel reporting.

- Prevent stockouts and overstock with AI demand forecasting
- Centralize pricing, promotions and loyalty programs
- Real-time sales dashboards across all stores and channels

[Get a demo](https://inovexa-erp.com/contact.html#form-section)

### Distribution

Run multi-depot distribution with route planning, warehouse automation, and stock levels by location.

- Plan delivery routes automatically to cut last-mile costs
- Track every pallet, SKU, and vehicle in real time
- Automate cross-docking and inter-depot transfers

[Get a demo](https://inovexa-erp.com/contact.html#form-section)

### Healthcare

Streamline clinic and hospital operations with HIPAA-compliant patient data management, medical inventory, and billing workflows.

- Manage medical supplies with expiry tracking and auto-reorder
- Automate staff scheduling across departments and shifts
- Simplify insurance claims and patient billing reconciliation

[Get a demo](https://inovexa-erp.com/contact.html#form-section)

### Professional Services

Track billable hours and project margins with built-in project management, resource planning, and client invoicing.

- Track project time, expenses, and margins in real time
- Automate recurring invoices and contract renewals
- 360° client CRM with full interaction history

[Get a demo](https://inovexa-erp.com/contact.html#form-section)

### Agribusiness

From farm to export - manage crop cycles, input costs, storage, and international trade compliance in a single platform.

- Track seasonal costs, yields, and profitability by plot
- Manage export documentation and trade certificates
- Multi-currency invoicing for international buyers

[Get a demo](https://inovexa-erp.com/contact.html#form-section)

## Tax rules and currencies for every country you sell in

Inovexa ERP supports custom tax rules and currencies for virtually every country.

### Custom Tax Engine

Configure any tax rule: Tunisian TVA, European VAT, UK VAT, US sales tax, withholding taxes, excise duties, and country-specific exemptions. Update rates without code changes.

### 180+ Currencies

Multi-currency invoicing, real-time exchange rates, and consolidated reporting in any currency. Invoice in TND, EUR, USD, GBP, SAR, AED, and any other currency your customers require.

### Country-Specific Compliance

Pre-configured for local fiscal rules, e-invoicing mandates, and statutory reporting formats in dozens of countries. New jurisdictions added continuously based on customer demand.

Don't see your country? [Talk to our team](https://inovexa-erp.com/contact.html). We add new jurisdictions based on customer demand.

Our Story

# Business software built in Tunis for companies everywhere

Inovexa was founded in Tunis in 2024 to give growing businesses the kind of ERP that used to be reserved for large corporations: finance, HR, supply chain, sales, and analytics in one cloud platform, at a price a small or mid-sized company can justify.

Founded in Tunis, 2024 Serving 12+ countries Part of MSAI Systems

Our Mission

## Serious ERP at a price growing businesses can afford

Growing companies need what large ones need: accurate books, payroll that runs on time, stock figures they can trust, and reports they can act on. We build those tools as modules, so a business can start with what it needs today and add more as it grows, wherever it operates.

Our Vision

## One ERP that works in any country

A company in Tunis, Toronto, or Nairobi should be able to run the same platform with its own tax rules, currency, and language. That is why every module we ship supports multiple countries, currencies, and languages from the start instead of having them added later.

What We Stand For

## Our Core Values

The principles we use when we decide what to build, how to price it, and how to support customers.

### Useful AI

We add AI where it saves measurable time, such as demand forecasting and spotting unusual transactions, and leave it out where it does not.

### Clear Pricing and Terms

No hidden fees and no surprise contracts. You know what you are getting, what it costs, and what is on our roadmap.

### Built for Real Teams

Teams work in French, Arabic, Spanish, or English, and screens are designed for warehouse and shop-floor staff as well as accountants.

### Less Hardware

Cloud deployment replaces on-premise servers that run around the clock, so there is less hardware to buy, power, and maintain.

By the Numbers

## Inovexa at a Glance

11

Founded in Tunis

Our Story

## From Tunisia to the World

Inovexa was born in 2024 in Tunis. Our founders had spent years watching Tunisian manufacturers, distributors, and growing companies struggle with fragmented tools: Excel spreadsheets, disconnected billing software, and manual HR processes. The problem wasn't a lack of ambition. It was a lack of the right tools.

We asked a simple question: why does a factory in Sfax have to use 1990s-era software while a startup in San Francisco gets AI-native ERP on day one? The answer was always cost and complexity. So we decided to solve both.

Today, Inovexa is part of [MSAI Systems](https://msai-systems.com) and serves businesses in more than 12 countries from its base in Tunis. The goal has not changed: the depth of a large ERP, with the setup time and price of a modern SaaS product.

24

2024 · Launch

#### Inovexa founded in Tunis

First modules launched: Finance, HR, and Sales CRM. First 10 clients onboarded within 6 months.

25

2025 · Expansion

#### First markets outside Tunisia

Expanded to Morocco, France, Spain, and Italy. Added Supply Chain, Production, and AI Engine modules.

26

2026 · Today

#### 11 modules in production

All 11 modules live, with AI features across finance, supply chain, and analytics. Customers in 12+ countries, interface in 3 languages.

Customers, resellers, technology partners, and engineers: tell us what you are working on and we will get back to you within 24 hours.

[Blog](https://inovexa-erp.com/blog.html) ERP Buyer's Guide

ERP Buyer's Guide

# The 20 Best ERP Software Systems in 2026, Compared

![Inovexa Team](https://inovexa-erp.com/logo.png) Inovexa Team

· October 15, 2026 · 14 min read

There is no single best ERP software for every company. What you can do is narrow the field quickly. This guide compares 20 ERP systems that buyers actually shortlist in 2026, grouped by the size of company they suit, with what each does well, where it falls short, how it is deployed and how it is priced.

We sell an ERP ourselves (Inovexa), so we have included it in the list and been as plain about its limits as about everyone else's. It is not at the top. For most of the products below, pricing is quote-based, so where we mention a number it is a published list price and should be checked with the vendor before you budget.

## How we grouped the best ERP software

Company size is the most useful first filter. We used three groups:

- **Enterprise:** large, often global companies with thousands of users, complex supply chains or heavy regulatory reporting. Projects usually run 12 months or longer with a systems integrator.
- **Mid-market:** companies from roughly 50 to 1,000 employees that have outgrown entry-level accounting software and need inventory, multi-entity finance or manufacturing.
- **SMB and open source:** smaller businesses, or teams with in-house technical skills that want low licence costs and control over the code.

## Enterprise ERP systems

### 1. SAP S/4HANA

**Best for:** large manufacturers, retailers and multinationals with complex operations across many countries.

S/4HANA covers almost every process a large company runs, with deep industry versions for areas such as oil and gas, automotive, utilities and consumer goods. The pool of SAP consultants worldwide is the largest of any ERP.

**Limitations:** projects are long and expensive, and you will depend on an integration partner. Many current customers are moving from the older SAP ECC because mainstream maintenance for ECC ends in 2027, which keeps experienced consultants busy and costly.

**Deployment:** cloud (sold through RISE with SAP), private cloud or on-premise. **Pricing:** quote-based subscription or licence.

### 2. Oracle Fusion Cloud ERP

**Best for:** large and upper mid-market companies that want a cloud-only finance and procurement platform.

Oracle's cloud suite is strong in financials, procurement, project accounting and enterprise performance management. It is delivered as true SaaS, with Oracle shipping updates every quarter, so customers stay on one version instead of planning big upgrade projects.

**Limitations:** quarterly updates mean regular regression testing. Licensing across the wider Oracle catalogue can be hard to read, and manufacturing depth is less of a reason to choose it than finance.

**Deployment:** Oracle-hosted cloud. **Pricing:** quote-based subscription.

### 3. Microsoft Dynamics 365 Finance and Supply Chain Management

**Best for:** large and upper mid-market manufacturers, distributors and retailers already using Microsoft 365 and Azure.

This is Microsoft's enterprise ERP, separate from Business Central. It handles multi-country finance, warehouse management, production planning and retail, and connects directly to Power BI, Power Automate and Teams. Microsoft's partner network is very large, so finding implementers in most countries is not hard.

**Limitations:** it is a large system that needs a capable partner, and Microsoft sets a minimum number of user licences. Costs climb as you add modules and add-on apps.

**Deployment:** Microsoft cloud. **Pricing:** Microsoft publishes per-user list prices; Finance has been listed at around $210 per user per month, with discounts for users who also take Supply Chain Management. Confirm current rates.

### 4. Infor CloudSuite

**Best for:** manufacturers and distributors in specific industries such as food and beverage, fashion, industrial equipment and automotive.

Infor sells industry-specific suites rather than one general product. CloudSuite Industrial (SyteLine), M3 and LN each target different types of manufacturing, and they come with a lot of sector functionality out of the box, which reduces custom development. The suites run on AWS.

**Limitations:** the product family is complicated to understand at first, and the partner ecosystem is smaller than SAP's or Microsoft's in many countries.

**Deployment:** multi-tenant cloud on AWS, with some on-premise options. **Pricing:** quote-based.

### 5. IFS Cloud

**Best for:** asset-heavy and project-based businesses: aerospace and defence, energy, construction, field service and equipment makers.

IFS combines ERP with enterprise asset management and field service management on one platform. If your revenue depends on maintaining equipment, running service contracts or delivering long projects, it covers that better than most general ERPs. IFS releases updates twice a year on a single codebase.

**Limitations:** it is more than a simple distributor or service business needs, and it is less widely known among smaller implementation partners.

**Deployment:** cloud or on-premise. **Pricing:** quote-based.

### 6. Workday Financial Management

**Best for:** services-heavy organisations, financial services, higher education and companies that already use Workday HCM.

Workday's strength is having finance and HR on the same data model. Headcount, payroll costs and financial planning line up without integration work, and reporting is fast.

**Limitations:** it is not built for manufacturing or complex inventory, so product companies usually look elsewhere. It sits at the top end on price.

**Deployment:** Workday cloud. **Pricing:** quote-based subscription.

## Mid-market ERP systems

### 7. Oracle NetSuite

**Best for:** fast-growing companies, especially SaaS, wholesale, e-commerce and services, that expect to add subsidiaries in other countries.

NetSuite was one of the first cloud ERPs and remains the default mid-market shortlist name. NetSuite OneWorld handles multiple subsidiaries, currencies and consolidations well, and the SuiteCloud platform allows deep customisation.

**Limitations:** costs grow with each module, user and edition, and renewal price increases are a common complaint. Serious customisation needs SuiteScript developers. We cover these costs in more detail in [our guide to hidden ERP costs](https://inovexa-erp.com/blog-erp-hidden-costs.html).

**Deployment:** Oracle cloud. **Pricing:** quote-based, usually an annual base licence plus per-user fees and modules.

### 8. Microsoft Dynamics 365 Business Central

**Best for:** small and mid-sized companies that live in Microsoft 365.

Business Central covers finance, sales, purchasing, inventory, projects and basic manufacturing. It works closely with Outlook, Excel and Teams, and the AppSource marketplace has thousands of add-ons for specific industries and countries. Partners exist almost everywhere.

**Limitations:** complex manufacturing and very high transaction volumes push it to its limits. Much of the real value comes from partner add-ons, each with its own fee.

**Deployment:** Microsoft cloud, or on-premise through a partner. **Pricing:** Microsoft publishes list prices; Essentials has been around $80 per user per month and Premium around $110. Implementation is extra.

### 9. Acumatica

**Best for:** mid-sized distributors, manufacturers and construction firms that want many users without per-seat fees.

Acumatica prices by the resources and transaction volume you use rather than by named users, so you can give access to occasional users without a licence bill. It has industry editions for distribution, manufacturing, construction and retail-commerce, and a modern browser interface.

**Limitations:** its partner network and customer base are concentrated in North America, so check local support if you operate elsewhere.

**Deployment:** cloud (SaaS or private cloud) or on-premise. **Pricing:** quote-based, by resource level and modules.

### 10. Sage Intacct

**Best for:** finance teams in services, non-profits, SaaS and healthcare that need strong multi-entity accounting.

Intacct is a cloud financial management system, and a good one. Its dimensional chart of accounts lets you report by department, location, project or grant without a huge account list, and multi-entity consolidation is fast.

**Limitations:** it is mainly a finance product. If you need manufacturing, warehouse management or deep inventory, you will be integrating other systems.

**Deployment:** cloud. **Pricing:** quote-based.

### 11. Epicor Kinetic

**Best for:** discrete and make-to-order manufacturers.

Kinetic has detailed production planning, scheduling, quality and shop-floor control, built for manufacturers that handle many product variants or jobs.

**Limitations:** service and distribution-only businesses rarely need its manufacturing depth and will find the project scope heavy.

**Deployment:** cloud or on-premise. **Pricing:** quote-based.

### 12. SAP Business One

**Best for:** small and mid-sized manufacturers and distributors, including subsidiaries of groups that run SAP at head office.

Business One is SAP's product for smaller companies. It covers finance, sales, purchasing, inventory and production, and is sold and supported by a large worldwide partner network. It can run on SAP HANA or Microsoft SQL Server.

**Limitations:** the experience depends heavily on your partner. Many industry needs are met through partner add-ons, and it is a different product from S/4HANA, so moving up later is a new implementation.

**Deployment:** on-premise or partner-hosted cloud. **Pricing:** quote-based through partners, as licence or subscription.

### 13. Sage X3

**Best for:** mid-sized manufacturers and distributors with several sites or countries, including process industries such as food and chemicals.

Sage X3 handles multi-site, multi-company and multi-currency operations, with traceability, lot control and process manufacturing features that matter in regulated sectors.

**Limitations:** results depend a lot on partner quality, and cloud options are less mature than those of products built for the cloud from the start.

**Deployment:** on-premise or hosted cloud. **Pricing:** quote-based through partners.

### 14. Unit4 ERPx

**Best for:** people-based organisations: professional services, public sector, non-profits and higher education.

Unit4 is built around people and projects rather than products. Time, expenses, resourcing, project accounting and grant management are central to the design.

**Limitations:** it is not a fit for companies with manufacturing or complex inventory.

**Deployment:** cloud. **Pricing:** quote-based.

### 15. Deltek

**Best for:** project-based firms: architecture and engineering, consultancies, agencies and government contractors.

Deltek has several products for different project businesses. Costpoint is widely used by US government contractors that need compliant cost accounting. Vantagepoint targets architecture and engineering firms, and Maconomy serves agencies and consultancies.

**Limitations:** each product is specialised, and Costpoint in particular is built around US government contracting rules.

**Deployment:** cloud or on-premise, depending on the product. **Pricing:** quote-based.

## SMB and open-source ERP

### 16. Odoo

**Best for:** small and mid-sized businesses that want to start with a few apps and add more over time.

Odoo, from Belgium, has a long list of apps covering accounting, inventory, manufacturing, CRM, e-commerce, HR and more, all on one database. The Community edition is open source and free. Enterprise adds features, hosting and support, with per-user pricing that varies by country and plan.

**Limitations:** heavy customisation can make major version upgrades painful. Some important features, including the full accounting app, are Enterprise only, and partner quality varies widely.

**Deployment:** Odoo Online, Odoo.sh or self-hosted. **Pricing:** Community free; Enterprise per user per month.

### 17. ERPNext

**Best for:** cost-conscious manufacturers, distributors and service firms with some in-house technical skill.

ERPNext is fully open source (GPL), built by Frappe on its own framework. It covers accounting, inventory, manufacturing, projects, HR and CRM, and all features are available without an enterprise edition.

**Limitations:** the partner network is smaller than the commercial vendors', and self-hosting means you are responsible for upgrades, backups and security.

**Deployment:** self-hosted or Frappe Cloud. **Pricing:** software free; hosting and support paid.

### 18. Zoho (Books, Inventory, Zoho One)

**Best for:** small businesses that want low-cost accounting, inventory and CRM from one vendor.

Zoho is not a single ERP, but its apps (Books, Inventory, CRM, People and others) connect well, and Zoho One bundles more than 40 of them. Pricing is published and low compared with most systems on this list.

**Limitations:** manufacturing is basic, and because these are separate apps, complex multi-entity or production scenarios outgrow it.

**Deployment:** Zoho cloud. **Pricing:** published; Books has a free tier in many regions and paid plans per organisation per month.

### 19. Sage 200

**Best for:** small and mid-sized businesses in the UK and Ireland.

Sage 200 covers finance, commercial, stock and project accounting, and a large number of UK accountants and resellers already know it.

**Limitations:** it is focused on the UK and Ireland, and parts of the architecture are older than cloud-native alternatives.

**Deployment:** on-premise or partner-hosted. **Pricing:** quote-based through partners.

### 20. Inovexa

**Best for:** growing SMEs and mid-sized companies operating in several countries.

Inovexa is a cloud ERP built in Tunis, Tunisia, and part of MSAI Systems. It has 11 modules (Dashboard, HR, Finance, Supply Chain, Production, Purchases, Sales & CRM, Logistics, AI Engine, Reports and Analytics) on one database. You pay for the modules you deploy, so a trading company can start with Finance, Purchases and Supply Chain and add Production or HR later. It handles multiple currencies and legal entities, runs in English and French, and is used by more than 340 companies in over 12 countries. A standard setup typically takes around 48 hours. See [our pricing page](https://inovexa-erp.com/pricing.html) for plans.

**Limitations:** Inovexa is a younger vendor with a smaller partner ecosystem than SAP, Microsoft or Oracle. It is not designed for very large enterprises with thousands of users and deep industry-specific requirements, where the products at the top of this list are a better fit.

**Deployment:** cloud. **Pricing:** modular, published on our pricing page.

## ERP comparison table

A quick summary of all 20 systems. "Quote-based" means there is no public list price and you will need to talk to the vendor or a partner.

| Product | Best for | Company size | Deployment | Pricing model |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| SAP S/4HANA | Complex global operations | Enterprise | Cloud, private cloud, on-premise | Quote-based |
| Oracle Fusion Cloud ERP | Cloud finance and procurement | Enterprise | Cloud | Quote-based |
| Dynamics 365 Finance & SCM | Microsoft-based manufacturers and distributors | Enterprise / upper mid-market | Cloud | Published per-user list price |
| Infor CloudSuite | Industry-specific manufacturing | Enterprise / mid-market | Cloud (AWS), some on-premise | Quote-based |
| IFS Cloud | Asset-heavy, service and project businesses | Enterprise / mid-market | Cloud or on-premise | Quote-based |
| Workday Financial Management | Services firms, finance plus HR | Enterprise | Cloud | Quote-based |
| Oracle NetSuite | Fast-growing multi-subsidiary companies | Mid-market | Cloud | Quote-based |
| Dynamics 365 Business Central | Microsoft 365 users | SMB / mid-market | Cloud or on-premise | Published per-user list price |
| Acumatica | Many users without per-seat fees | Mid-market | Cloud or on-premise | Quote-based, by resources |
| Sage Intacct | Multi-entity finance teams | SMB / mid-market | Cloud | Quote-based |
| Epicor Kinetic | Discrete and make-to-order manufacturing | Mid-market | Cloud or on-premise | Quote-based |
| SAP Business One | SMB manufacturers and distributors | SMB / mid-market | On-premise or hosted | Quote-based via partners |
| Sage X3 | Multi-site manufacturing and distribution | Mid-market | On-premise or hosted | Quote-based via partners |
| Unit4 ERPx | Services, public sector, non-profits | Mid-market / enterprise | Cloud | Quote-based |
| Deltek | Project-based firms, government contractors | Mid-market | Cloud or on-premise | Quote-based |
| Odoo | Starting small and adding apps | SMB / mid-market | Cloud or self-hosted | Community free; Enterprise per user |
| ERPNext | Open source with in-house tech skills | SMB | Self-hosted or Frappe Cloud | Free software; paid hosting |
| Zoho (Books, Inventory, One) | Low-cost small business apps | Small business | Cloud | Published, low monthly plans |
| Sage 200 | UK and Ireland SMBs | SMB | On-premise or hosted | Quote-based via partners |
| Inovexa | Growing multi-country SMEs | SMB / mid-market | Cloud | Modular, published pricing |

## How to choose the right ERP software

These criteria will remove most of the wrong options. For a fuller process, see [our step-by-step guide to choosing an ERP](https://inovexa-erp.com/blog-how-to-choose-erp.html).

### Start with your core process, not the feature list

Write down the process that makes you money: make-to-order production, project delivery, importing and reselling, subscription billing. Then shortlist systems built around that process. A project firm should look at Unit4 or Deltek before a manufacturing system, and a job-shop manufacturer should look at Epicor before Workday.

### Count entities, currencies and countries

If you invoice in more than one currency or run more than one legal entity, test consolidation and intercompany transactions in the demo with your own data. This is where many entry-level systems break. Our article on [multi-currency ERP](https://inovexa-erp.com/blog-multi-currency-erp.html) lists what to check.

### Check local tax and e-invoicing support

Ask each vendor which countries they support natively for VAT, payroll and e-invoicing, and which depend on a partner add-on. A missing localisation is expensive to build.

### Work out the three-year cost

Add licences, implementation, data migration, training, add-ons and internal staff time over three years. Implementation often costs as much as or more than the first years of licences on the larger systems.

### Look at the partner, not only the product

For SAP, Microsoft, Sage and Odoo, the partner does most of the work. Ask for two references of similar size and industry, and speak to them without the partner present.

### Be realistic about time to go live

Enterprise projects commonly take a year or more; mid-market projects often take three to nine months. If you need to be live by a fixed date, such as a new financial year, tell vendors upfront and ask what they would cut. Our [ERP implementation guide](https://inovexa-erp.com/blog-erp-implementation-guide.html) covers typical timelines.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is the best ERP software in 2026?

There is no single best ERP for every company. For large multinationals, SAP S/4HANA, Oracle Fusion Cloud ERP and Microsoft Dynamics 365 Finance and Supply Chain Management are the usual shortlist. For mid-sized companies, NetSuite, Dynamics 365 Business Central and Acumatica are common choices. Smaller businesses often look at Odoo, ERPNext or Zoho. The right choice depends on your core process, number of entities and countries, and budget.

### How much does ERP software cost?

Most enterprise and mid-market ERP vendors use quote-based pricing. Some publish list prices: Microsoft lists Dynamics 365 Business Central Essentials at around $80 per user per month, for example. Implementation, data migration, training and add-ons often add as much as or more than the licence cost, so compare the total cost over three years rather than the monthly fee.

### What is the best ERP for small businesses?

Small businesses usually do well with Dynamics 365 Business Central, Odoo, Zoho, ERPNext or SAP Business One, depending on whether they need manufacturing, how much technical skill they have in-house and which software they already use. If you trade in several countries or currencies, check multi-currency and multi-entity support early.

### Is open-source ERP a good option?

Open-source ERP such as Odoo Community and ERPNext can keep licence costs low and give you control over the code. The trade-off is that you or a partner are responsible for hosting, upgrades, security and support. It suits companies with some in-house technical capacity or a reliable local partner.

### How long does an ERP implementation take?

Enterprise ERP projects commonly take a year or more. Mid-market projects often take three to nine months. Smaller cloud ERP setups with standard processes can be live in days or weeks. Data quality, customisation and how many sites go live at once have the biggest effect on the timeline.

### Cloud ERP or on-premise ERP: which should I choose?

Most new ERP projects in 2026 are cloud-based, because the vendor handles hosting, updates and security, and costs are spread over a subscription. On-premise still makes sense where regulation, data residency rules or existing infrastructure require it. Several vendors on this list, such as Epicor, IFS and Acumatica, offer both.

### Is Inovexa on your shortlist?

If you run a growing business across more than one country and want finance, purchasing, stock and production on one database, Inovexa is worth a look. You choose the modules you need and add others later.

Book a demo and we will walk through your own process, including multi-currency and multi-entity setup. If another system on this list fits you better, we will tell you.

ERP Comparison

# 10 Best NetSuite Alternatives in 2026 for Growing Businesses

![Inovexa Team](https://inovexa-erp.com/logo.png) Inovexa Team

· October 15, 2026 · 12 min read

NetSuite is a capable cloud ERP, and plenty of companies run on it for years without regret. It is also one of the systems finance teams most often start replacing around the second or third renewal. If you are reading about NetSuite alternatives, you probably have a specific reason. Below are ten options, who each suits, where each falls short, and how to move your data cleanly.

We sell one of the products on this list (Inovexa). We have put it at number ten, not number one, and we have tried to be as plain about its limits as about everyone else's.

## Why companies look for NetSuite alternatives

The same reasons come up again and again. None mean NetSuite is a bad product; most come from how it is packaged and sold.

- **Renewal increases.** NetSuite is sold on annual or multi-year subscriptions. Many customers report that the renewal quote came in noticeably higher than the original, especially once first-term discounts fell away. Whether a cap applies depends entirely on what your contract says.
- **Per-user plus module pricing.** The bill is built from a base platform licence, user licences and add-on modules such as OneWorld, Advanced Revenue Management or WMS. Every new hire who needs a login and every new capability adds a line item.
- **Customization means SuiteScript.** SuiteFlow covers many workflows without code. Beyond that, changes are written in SuiteScript, NetSuite's JavaScript-based language. You need a developer, in-house or from a partner, and scripts need retesting around NetSuite's twice-yearly releases.
- **Implementation partner cost.** The licence is only part of the spend. Implementation, later optimization work and ongoing admin support are separate, and they add up. We break this down in [the hidden costs of ERP](https://inovexa-erp.com/blog-erp-hidden-costs.html).
- **Fit for small teams.** A 15-person company with one entity and simple inventory can end up paying for a platform built for much larger, more complex organizations.

## Who should stay on NetSuite

Switching ERP is expensive and disruptive. Before you start, be honest about whether the problem is the product or the contract. NetSuite is probably still the right call if:

- You run several subsidiaries in different countries and rely on OneWorld for consolidation and intercompany eliminations.
- Your implementation works, your team knows the system, and your complaint is mostly price. A firm renewal negotiation, or dropping unused licences and modules, may solve it for far less than a migration.
- You have years of SuiteScript customizations that encode real business logic and would need to be rebuilt elsewhere.
- You are scaling fast toward an audit, fundraise or IPO and want a system auditors and investors already know well.

If none of that describes you, the alternatives below are worth a look.

## 1. Microsoft Dynamics 365 Business Central

**Best for:** small and mid-sized companies already using Microsoft 365, Teams and Power BI.

**Why it is a NetSuite alternative:** it covers similar ground (finance, sales, purchasing, inventory, light manufacturing, projects) as a cloud SaaS product, and it is sold through a very large partner network, so you have real choice when picking an implementer.

**Limitations:** most deployments depend on a partner for setup and localization. Deeper changes are built as extensions in AL, Microsoft's own language, so you swap one specialist skill set for another.

**Pricing model:** per user per month, with Essentials and Premium tiers published on Microsoft's website. Partner services are quoted separately.

**Migration notes:** data comes in through configuration packages (Excel-based templates). Ask your partner whether they have moved a NetSuite customer before, since there is no one-click route.

## 2. Acumatica

**Best for:** distributors, manufacturers, construction firms and other growing companies where many people need occasional access.

**Why it is a NetSuite alternative:** Acumatica does not charge per user. Pricing is based on the modules you choose and the transaction volume and resources you consume, with unlimited users. If your NetSuite bill grows mostly because more staff need logins, that changes the maths directly. It also offers industry editions for distribution, manufacturing and construction.

**Limitations:** it is sold and implemented through partners, and the ecosystem is smaller than Microsoft's or NetSuite's. Check partner references.

**Pricing model:** quote-based, built on modules plus resource level.

**Migration notes:** Acumatica has import scenarios for loading data from Excel or CSV. Plan the chart of accounts and subaccount structure early, as it works differently from NetSuite segments.

## 3. Sage Intacct

**Best for:** finance-led organizations such as SaaS companies, professional services firms, nonprofits and multi-entity groups.

**Why it is a NetSuite alternative:** it is a finance-first system. Its dimensional general ledger, multi-entity consolidation and reporting are the main reason people buy it. Many companies that used NetSuite mostly as an accounting platform find Intacct a closer match to what they actually use.

**Limitations:** it is not a full operations suite. Manufacturing and complex inventory usually need a separate system connected through its marketplace or API.

**Pricing model:** quote-based, depending on modules, entities and users.

**Migration notes:** map NetSuite classes, departments and locations to Intacct dimensions before you load anything.

## 4. SAP Business One

**Best for:** small and mid-sized manufacturers and distributors, and subsidiaries of groups that run SAP at head office.

**Why it is a NetSuite alternative:** it covers finance, purchasing, inventory, production and sales in one product, has a long track record, and has a large partner network in many countries. For a subsidiary that needs to report into a parent's SAP environment, it is often the easiest political and technical fit.

**Limitations:** it was designed as an on-premise product. Cloud deployments are usually hosted by partners rather than delivered as multi-tenant SaaS, and the user interface feels older than newer cloud systems.

**Pricing model:** user licences by type, sold through partners, either perpetual or subscription. Quote-based.

**Migration notes:** partners typically use the Data Transfer Workbench or their own tools to load master data and opening balances.

## 5. Odoo

**Best for:** small and mid-sized companies that want a wide set of apps at a predictable price and are comfortable with some configuration work.

**Why it is a NetSuite alternative:** Odoo covers accounting, inventory, manufacturing, CRM, e-commerce, HR and more, and you switch on only the apps you need. It publishes its per-user pricing openly, which makes budgeting simple. There is also an open-source Community edition, and customization is done in Python, a widely known language.

**Limitations:** depth varies from app to app. Heavily customized instances can take real work to upgrade between versions, and partner quality is uneven.

**Pricing model:** published per-user monthly pricing for Enterprise, with hosting options. Implementation partners charge separately.

**Migration notes:** Odoo imports CSV and Excel files for most objects. Keep customizations small in the first phase and add them once the core is stable.

## 6. Epicor Kinetic

**Best for:** discrete and make-to-order manufacturers.

**Why it is a NetSuite alternative:** NetSuite's manufacturing features cover many assembly and work-order scenarios, but shops with complex routings, shop-floor data collection, quality control and product configurators often need more. Kinetic is built around those processes.

**Limitations:** it is a manufacturing system first. Service businesses and pure distributors will pay for depth they do not use, and implementations are larger projects.

**Pricing model:** quote-based, cloud subscription or on-premise.

**Migration notes:** the hard part is not finance data. It is bills of materials, routings and work centres, which often have to be rebuilt rather than imported, because NetSuite may never have held them at that level of detail.

## 7. Infor CloudSuite Industrial (SyteLine)

**Best for:** mid-sized and larger manufacturers, especially in configure-to-order and engineer-to-order environments.

**Why it is a NetSuite alternative:** like Epicor, it goes further into production planning, scheduling and shop-floor control than a general-purpose ERP.

**Limitations:** the sales and implementation process is closer to enterprise software than to a quick SaaS rollout. Expect a longer project and a bigger internal team commitment.

**Pricing model:** quote-based subscription.

**Migration notes:** treat it as a manufacturing transformation, not a finance swap.

## 8. Workday Financials

**Best for:** larger services-based organizations, especially those already using Workday HCM.

**Why it is a NetSuite alternative:** companies that outgrow NetSuite on the finance side sometimes move up to Workday, particularly when HR and finance want one system for people, cost and planning data.

**Limitations:** it is aimed at large organizations and is rarely a cost-saving move. It is not designed for inventory-heavy or manufacturing businesses.

**Pricing model:** quote-based subscription, usually sized on employee count.

**Migration notes:** implementations are run by Workday or certified partners with a structured methodology.

## 9. Zoho (Books, Inventory, One)

**Best for:** small companies that adopted NetSuite early, or are considering it, and have simple operations.

**Why it is a NetSuite alternative:** for a small team, Zoho Books plus Zoho Inventory covers invoicing, bills, bank feeds, multi-currency and stock. Zoho One bundles a large number of Zoho apps (CRM, Books, Inventory, People and more) under one subscription. Pricing is published and low compared with mid-market ERP.

**Limitations:** you will feel the limits with multiple entities, complex consolidation, or manufacturing.

**Pricing model:** published monthly plans. Zoho Books has a free tier for very small businesses, and Zoho One is priced per employee or per user.

**Migration notes:** import contacts, items and open invoices by CSV, and bring in opening balances rather than full transaction history.

## 10. Inovexa

**Best for:** small and mid-sized companies with cross-border operations that want to pay only for the modules they use.

**Why it is a NetSuite alternative:** Inovexa is a cloud ERP built in Tunis, Tunisia, and part of MSAI Systems. It has 11 modules (Dashboard, HR, Finance, Supply Chain, Production, Purchases, Sales & CRM, Logistics, AI Engine, Reports and Analytics) running on one database. Pricing is modular: you pay for the modules you deploy, not for a full suite. It handles multiple currencies, multiple entities, and English and French. More than 340 companies in 12+ countries use it, and a typical standard setup takes about 48 hours. We also help with data migration.

**Limitations:** we are a younger vendor than anyone else on this list. Our partner network and third-party app ecosystem are much smaller than NetSuite's, Microsoft's or SAP's. If you need a large local implementation partner in your city, or a marketplace with hundreds of ready-made connectors, check that we cover what you need before you commit. The 48-hour figure is for a standard setup; migrating years of history and custom processes takes longer.

**Pricing model:** modular, per deployed module. See the [pricing page](https://inovexa-erp.com/pricing.html) or ask for a quote.

**Migration notes:** our team helps load master data, opening balances and open transactions. Start with Finance and the modules you rely on daily, and add the rest once the core is live. If you run in several currencies, our guide to [multi-currency ERP](https://inovexa-erp.com/blog-multi-currency-erp.html) covers what to check.

## How to migrate off NetSuite

Most failed migrations go wrong on planning, not software. The checklist below is what we would want in place before any cutover. For the broader project view, see our [ERP implementation timeline](https://inovexa-erp.com/blog-erp-implementation-guide.html) and the list of [common implementation mistakes](https://inovexa-erp.com/blog-erp-implementation-failures.html).

1. **Find your contract renewal date first.** Read the notice terms. Work back from that date so you are not forced into another full term, or into a short extension at a worse rate, because the new system is not ready.
2. **Export everything while you still have full access.** Use saved searches to export records to CSV or Excel, and NetSuite's Full CSV Export for a broad snapshot. Download File Cabinet attachments separately. Keep copies of your SuiteScripts and workflow definitions as documentation, even though they will not run elsewhere.
3. **Map the chart of accounts.** Decide whether to keep your account structure or clean it up. Map NetSuite subsidiaries, classes, departments and locations to whatever the new system uses (dimensions, subaccounts, entities). Get your accountant to sign off on the mapping.
4. **Handle open transactions explicitly.** Open customer invoices, unpaid vendor bills, open purchase and sales orders, and deferred revenue schedules need to be recreated in the new system with their original dates and amounts, so aging reports and cash forecasts stay correct.
5. **Decide how much history to bring.** Most companies load opening balances plus one or two years of summarized monthly balances, and archive the full detail. Moving every historical transaction is slow and rarely needed day to day.
6. **Run in parallel for at least one month-end close.** Process the same period in both systems and reconcile trial balances, AR and AP. Differences are cheap to fix here, not after cutover.
7. **Time the cutover.** Go live at the start of a fiscal period, ideally a quarter or year start, and outside your busiest season. Leave a buffer between go-live and the NetSuite contract end date for final reconciliations and extracts.

Before you sign anything

- Ask each vendor for a reference customer who moved from NetSuite.
- Get a written three-year cost, including implementation and support.
- Confirm who owns your data and how you export it if you leave later.
- List which NetSuite customizations you still use.

If you have not done a structured selection before, our step-by-step guide on [how to choose an ERP](https://inovexa-erp.com/blog-how-to-choose-erp.html) walks through requirements, demos and scoring.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is the best NetSuite alternative for a small business?

For small teams with simple operations, Zoho (Books, Inventory or One) and Odoo are the most common choices because their pricing is published and lower. If you already run on Microsoft 365, Business Central is worth a demo. Inovexa suits small companies with cross-border trade that want to buy only the modules they need.

### Which NetSuite alternative is closest for multi-entity accounting?

Sage Intacct is the usual answer for finance-led companies that need consolidation across entities. Business Central and Acumatica also handle multiple companies. If you rely heavily on NetSuite OneWorld across many countries, compare carefully before you leave.

### Which NetSuite alternative is best for manufacturers?

Epicor Kinetic and Infor CloudSuite Industrial are built for manufacturing, with deeper shop-floor, scheduling and quality features. Acumatica's Manufacturing Edition and SAP Business One suit smaller manufacturers. Odoo and Inovexa include production modules for less complex operations.

### How long does it take to migrate off NetSuite?

It depends on scope. A single-entity, finance-focused move can take a few weeks. A multi-entity business with inventory, manufacturing and custom scripts can take several months.

### Can I export my data from NetSuite?

Yes. Saved searches export records to CSV or Excel, and the Full CSV Export gives a broad snapshot of your account. Attachments in the File Cabinet are downloaded separately. SuiteScripts can be saved as documentation but will need rebuilding in the new system.

### When should I start planning a move away from NetSuite?

Start at least two quarters before your renewal date. That leaves time to choose a system, migrate, run a parallel close and cut over without being pushed into another full NetSuite term.

Open Source Buyer's Guide

# 12 Best Open-Source ERP Systems in 2026 (Free and Self-Hosted)

![Inovexa Team](https://inovexa-erp.com/logo.png) Inovexa Team

· October 15, 2026 · 12 min read

If you are searching for the **best open source ERP**, you will find plenty of lists that rate everything five stars. This one covers 12 open-source ERP systems that are still in use in 2026, what each one is good at, where it falls short, and what it really costs to run one yourself.

A note on who is writing: Inovexa is a hosted cloud ERP, not an open-source product. Near the end we explain when a hosted system is the better call and when it is not.

## What "open source ERP" actually means

Open source means the code is published under a license that lets you read, run, modify and usually redistribute it. Many of the systems below follow an "open core" model: a free community edition plus a paid edition with extra modules, hosting or support.

Three questions matter more than the label:

- **Which license?** Permissive licenses (Apache 2.0) let you do almost anything. Copyleft licenses (GPL, AGPL) require you to share modifications under certain conditions. LGPL sits in between.
- **Which features are in the free edition?** Some vendors keep accounting reports, mobile apps or the upgrade tooling in the paid tier.
- **Who will run it?** Someone has to install it, patch it, back it up and upgrade it. That person costs money even when the software does not.

## The 12 best open source ERP systems in 2026

### 1. Odoo (Community vs Enterprise)

Odoo is the most widely used open-source ERP and the one most buyers look at first. It covers accounting, sales, CRM, inventory, manufacturing, purchasing, projects, HR, a website builder and eCommerce, all as separate apps you switch on.

**License:** Odoo Community is LGPLv3. Odoo Enterprise is proprietary and sold per user. **Stack:** Python, PostgreSQL, a JavaScript front end.

The split between editions is the thing to understand before you start. Community is a real, usable product, but several features people expect are Enterprise-only, including Odoo Studio, the official mobile apps and parts of the full accounting suite. Odoo's own hosting (Odoo Online and Odoo.sh) is tied to Enterprise subscriptions, so Community users self-host or use a partner.

Upgrades are the other catch. Odoo ships a major version every year, and moving a Community database with custom modules from one major version to the next is a project, not a button. The Odoo Community Association (OCA) maintains a large library of free modules and migration tools that fill many gaps.

**Best for:** small and mid-sized companies that want broad coverage and have a developer or partner on call. **Hosting:** self-hosted, partner-hosted, or Odoo's cloud if you move to Enterprise.

### 2. ERPNext (Frappe)

ERPNext is built on the Frappe Framework by Frappe Technologies in India. It covers accounting, stock, buying, selling, manufacturing, projects and assets. HR and payroll now live in a separate Frappe HR app.

**License:** GPLv3, and the full product is open. There is no locked enterprise edition. **Stack:** Python and JavaScript on Frappe, MariaDB as the main database.

Its strengths are a clean data model, good manufacturing basics (BOMs, work orders, job cards) and a built-in way to add custom fields, forms and scripts without forking the code. Frappe Cloud offers managed hosting from the people who build it.

Limitations: localization outside India and a handful of other countries depends on community apps of uneven quality. Advanced warehouse logic and complex multi-company consolidation need work. Major upgrades are smoother than Odoo's but still need testing if you have custom apps.

**Best for:** small manufacturers and distributors that want a fully open product with no paid tier to grow into. **Hosting:** self-hosted, Frappe Cloud, or partners.

### 3. Dolibarr

Dolibarr is a PHP application aimed at small businesses, freelancers and associations. It is very popular in France and Belgium. You turn modules on from a settings page: third parties, proposals, orders, invoices, stock, projects, HR leave, a basic MRP, and so on.

**License:** GPLv3 or later. **Stack:** PHP with MySQL or MariaDB (PostgreSQL is also supported).

It runs on cheap shared hosting and is easy to learn. The DoliStore marketplace sells extra modules, and DoliCloud provides official hosting. The trade-off is depth: accounting is fine for a small company but not for group consolidation, and manufacturing and warehouse features are basic.

**Best for:** very small businesses that want quotes, invoices, stock and projects in one place without paying per user.

### 4. Apache OFBiz

OFBiz (Open For Business) is an Apache Software Foundation project. It ships with accounting, order management, catalog, manufacturing, warehouse and eCommerce components, but it is better described as a framework for building an ERP than a finished product.

**License:** Apache 2.0. **Stack:** Java, Groovy, its own entity engine on top of a relational database (Derby by default, with PostgreSQL or MySQL in production).

The permissive license is the main draw: you can build a commercial product on it without sharing your changes. The downside is a dated stock interface, substantial Java work in most real deployments, and no single vendor offering support.

**Best for:** companies or software vendors with Java developers who want a base to build on.

### 5. iDempiere

iDempiere is a community fork of ADempiere, rebuilt on OSGi so that plugins can be added without touching the core. It is strong on accounting, multi-organization structures, and a configurable application dictionary that lets you define windows and fields without code.

**License:** GPLv2. **Stack:** Java, OSGi, ZK web UI, PostgreSQL or Oracle.

It handles multiple clients, organizations and currencies well, and its double-entry accounting is thorough. The learning curve is steep, the UI shows its age, and support comes from a network of independent implementers rather than one company.

**Best for:** distribution and multi-entity businesses with access to an experienced iDempiere partner.

### 6. Tryton

Tryton started in 2008 as a fork of TinyERP/OpenERP (now Odoo) and has been governed by a non-profit foundation since. It offers accounting, sales, purchasing, stock, production, projects and more as separate modules.

**License:** GPLv3. **Stack:** Python, PostgreSQL, a desktop client and a web client.

Tryton's appeal is engineering discipline. It runs on a predictable release schedule with long-term support versions, and upgrades between versions are designed to be manageable. There is no paid edition holding features back.

The ecosystem is smaller than Odoo's and the interface is plain. You will want a developer or a Tryton service provider.

**Best for:** technically capable teams that care more about stable upgrades than about a large app store.

### 7. Axelor

Axelor is a French company whose Axelor Open Suite sits on a low-code platform. It covers CRM, sales, purchasing, stock, production, accounting, HR and projects, with a studio for building forms and workflows.

**License:** AGPLv3 for Axelor Open Suite. **Stack:** Java, PostgreSQL.

The low-code tools are the main reason to choose it. Business analysts can add fields, views and BPMN workflows without Java work. Documentation and community activity are thinner than Odoo's, and much of it is French-first. The AGPL license also matters if you plan to offer a modified version as a hosted service.

**Best for:** mid-sized French-speaking companies that want to configure processes heavily. **Hosting:** self-hosted or through Axelor and its partners.

### 8. metasfresh

metasfresh comes from metas GmbH in Germany and is another descendant of the ADempiere code base, heavily reworked. It is used mostly in wholesale, distribution and food businesses.

**License:** GPL. **Stack:** Java, PostgreSQL, a web UI alongside the older Swing client.

It handles high order volumes, EDI, traceability and procurement contracts well, which explains its following in food trading. Outside German-speaking markets the partner network is small, and some documentation assumes German context.

**Best for:** wholesalers and food distributors, especially in the DACH region.

### 9. ADempiere

ADempiere was forked from Compiere in 2006 and is the ancestor of iDempiere and metasfresh. It is still maintained, with work on a newer web interface.

**License:** GPLv2. **Stack:** Java, PostgreSQL or Oracle.

It shares the strengths of its family, but most of the community energy moved to iDempiere years ago. If you are starting fresh, compare the two directly.

**Best for:** organizations already running ADempiere, or working with a partner who specializes in it.

### 10. Openbravo

Openbravo, from Spain, was one of the best-known web-based open-source ERPs in the late 2000s. Since then the company has shifted to a commercial, cloud-based retail and point-of-sale platform. The community ERP edition still exists, but it receives little new development.

**Stack:** Java, PostgreSQL or Oracle, web UI.

For a new general ERP project in 2026 we would not start here. Its history is a useful warning: an open-source product can change direction when the company behind it does.

**Best for:** retailers evaluating Openbravo's commercial platform, or companies maintaining an existing install.

### 11. xTuple (PostBooks)

xTuple, based in the United States, offers a free open-source edition historically called PostBooks, plus paid Distribution and Manufacturing editions. The free edition covers accounting, CRM, sales, purchasing and basic inventory.

**License:** the open edition is under the CPAL. **Stack:** PostgreSQL with much of the business logic in the database, a Qt desktop client and a web client.

The accounting is good, and putting logic in PostgreSQL makes reporting straightforward. Manufacturing features such as MRP sit in the paid editions, and localization is US-centric.

**Best for:** small US distributors and light manufacturers that are comfortable with a desktop client.

### 12. LedgerSMB

LedgerSMB began in 2006 as a fork of SQL-Ledger. It is accounting-first: general ledger, AR, AP, invoicing, basic inventory, quotations and orders. It is not a full ERP, and it does not pretend to be.

**License:** GPLv2. **Stack:** Perl, PostgreSQL.

It is a sensible choice when your real need is reliable bookkeeping with some order handling and you want your data in a well-structured PostgreSQL database. It has no manufacturing, CRM or HR to speak of.

**Best for:** small firms that need open-source accounting more than a full ERP.

## Comparison table

| System | Best for | License | Stack | Paid tier |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Odoo Community | Broad SME coverage | LGPLv3 | Python, PostgreSQL | Yes (Enterprise) |
| ERPNext | Small manufacturing, distribution | GPLv3 | Python, MariaDB | Hosting only |
| Dolibarr | Very small businesses | GPLv3+ | PHP, MySQL | Add-ons, hosting |
| Apache OFBiz | Custom builds | Apache 2.0 | Java | No |
| iDempiere | Multi-entity, distribution | GPLv2 | Java, PostgreSQL | Partner services |
| Tryton | Stable, long-lived installs | GPLv3 | Python, PostgreSQL | Partner services |
| Axelor | Low-code configuration | AGPLv3 | Java, PostgreSQL | Yes |
| metasfresh | Wholesale, food | GPL | Java, PostgreSQL | Hosting, support |
| ADempiere | Existing installs | GPLv2 | Java, PostgreSQL | Partner services |
| Openbravo | Retail (commercial) | Varies by edition | Java | Yes, main focus |
| xTuple | US distribution | CPAL (open edition) | PostgreSQL, Qt | Yes |
| LedgerSMB | Accounting only | GPLv2 | Perl, PostgreSQL | No |

## The true cost of a "free" ERP

The license fee is zero. The project is not. Here is where the money goes, roughly in the order you will meet it. We cover the general version of this in our piece on [hidden ERP costs](https://inovexa-erp.com/blog-erp-hidden-costs.html), but open source shifts the weight in specific ways.

- **Hosting.** A server, a managed database or a VPS, plus offsite backups and monitoring. Small for one company, but it never stops, and someone has to be responsible when the disk fills up on a Friday night.
- **Implementation.** Setting up the chart of accounts, tax rules, warehouses, units of measure, price lists and user roles, then migrating opening balances and master data. This is the same work as with a commercial ERP, and it is usually the largest single cost. Our [implementation timeline guide](https://inovexa-erp.com/blog-erp-implementation-guide.html) shows what a realistic schedule looks like.
- **Customization.** Open source makes it easy to change the code, which makes it easy to change too much. Every custom module is something you will have to port to the next version.
- **Upgrades.** This is the cost most teams underestimate. With Odoo Community, for example, skipping two or three major versions and then trying to catch up can mean weeks of developer time. Budget for upgrades every year, or accept that you will stay on an old version.
- **Security patches.** You apply them, test them and schedule the downtime. Nobody does it for you.
- **Support.** Community forums are helpful but have no response time. When payroll will not post the day before payday, you want a contract with someone.
- **Local compliance.** E-invoicing formats, tax reports and statutory accounts change by country and by year. If your country's localization is maintained by two volunteers, that is a risk you are taking on.

A practical test: price three years of a self-hosted install, including implementation and one upgrade, against three years of a hosted subscription. Sometimes open source wins clearly. Sometimes the gap is much smaller than "free" suggests.

## When open source is the wrong choice

Open-source ERP is a good fit when you have technical people, specific processes that off-the-shelf software handles badly, and a reason to own the code. It is a poor fit in these situations:

- **No one in-house can own it.** If your plan is "the accountant's nephew will set it up," expect trouble in year two.
- **You need it running in weeks.** A self-hosted install that is configured, migrated and tested takes longer than most teams expect. Our list of [common ERP implementation mistakes](https://inovexa-erp.com/blog-erp-implementation-failures.html) covers why.
- **Your country's localization is weak.** Check who maintains the tax and e-invoicing modules for your country and when they last released.
- **You want predictable costs.** Self-hosting turns a fixed subscription into a series of variable bills for servers, developers and upgrades.
- **Auditors or customers ask for certifications.** You become responsible for documenting security controls on the servers you run.

## When a hosted modular cloud ERP makes more sense

To be clear, Inovexa is not open source. It is a cloud ERP built in Tunis, Tunisia, and part of MSAI Systems. We host it, patch it and upgrade it. You do not get the source code, and you cannot fork it. If owning the code matters to you, one of the 12 systems above is the right direction.

Where a hosted option like ours tends to fit better is when the reasons people choose open source are really about cost and flexibility, not code ownership:

- **You only want to pay for what you use.** Inovexa has 11 modules (Dashboard, HR, Finance, Supply Chain, Production, Purchases, Sales & CRM, Logistics, AI Engine, Reports, Analytics) on one database, and you pay for the modules you deploy. That is the same idea as switching on apps in Odoo or Dolibarr, without running the server. Our article on [modular ERP](https://inovexa-erp.com/blog-composable-erp-modular.html) explains the approach.
- **You do not have an IT team.** A typical standard setup takes about 48 hours. There is no upgrade project to plan.
- **You run several entities or currencies.** Multi-currency and multi-entity are built in rather than added through community modules.

Inovexa is used by more than 340 companies in over 12 countries. It is not the right choice for everyone, and for a company with strong developers and unusual processes, a well-run Odoo or ERPNext install can be the better answer. If you are unsure, our [step-by-step guide to choosing an ERP](https://inovexa-erp.com/blog-how-to-choose-erp.html) is a neutral place to start.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is the best open source ERP for a small business?

For most small businesses the shortlist is Odoo Community, ERPNext and Dolibarr. Dolibarr is the simplest to run. ERPNext is fully open with no paid tier. Odoo has the widest range of apps, but some features are in the paid Enterprise edition.

### Is Odoo really open source?

Odoo Community is open source under LGPLv3. Odoo Enterprise is a proprietary, paid edition with extra features such as Studio and the official mobile apps. Many companies start on Community and later move to Enterprise.

### Is ERPNext completely free?

The software is free and licensed under GPLv3, with no locked features. You still pay for hosting, implementation and support, either to Frappe through Frappe Cloud, to a partner, or in your own staff time.

### Can I self-host an open-source ERP on my own server?

Yes. All 12 systems in this list can be self-hosted. You become responsible for backups, security updates, uptime and version upgrades, so plan for that work before you install.

### How much does an open-source ERP cost to run?

The license is free, but hosting, implementation, customization, upgrades and support are not. Implementation is usually the largest cost. Compare three years of total cost, not license price, before deciding.

### Is Inovexa an open-source ERP?

No. Inovexa is a hosted cloud ERP. You do not get the source code. You pay for the modules you deploy, and we handle hosting, updates and upgrades.

Integrations

# 20 Apps Worth Connecting to Your ERP in 2026

![Inovexa Team](https://inovexa-erp.com/logo.png) Inovexa Team

· October 15, 2026 · 12 min read

Most ERP integrations exist for one reason: someone was retyping data from one screen into another. An order arrives in Shopify, a payout lands from Stripe, a deal closes in HubSpot, and each time a person copies numbers into the ERP and hopes they got them right. This guide covers 20 apps that integrate with ERP systems and are worth connecting, grouped by category. For each: what data moves, which way, how often, and what breaks without it.

One note first: work inside the ERP should not need an integration at all. In [Inovexa](https://inovexa-erp.com/products.html), the 11 modules share one database, so a sales order, the stock it reserves and the invoice it produces are the same records seen from different screens. Integrations are for the apps outside that boundary.

## Payments and banking

### 1. Stripe

**Data flow:** Stripe to ERP. Charges, refunds, disputes, fees and payouts. Charges usually come through webhooks in near real time; payouts are reconciled when they hit the bank.

A good setup posts each charge against the customer invoice, records the Stripe fee as an expense, and books the payout net of fees to a bank clearing account. Without the integration, someone gets a single payout of, say, 4,812.37 and has to work out which 60 invoices it covers and why it is short by the fees.

### 2. PayPal

**Data flow:** PayPal to ERP. Transactions, fees, refunds, currency conversions and transfers to your bank, usually pulled daily through PayPal's transaction reporting.

PayPal behaves like a bank account with its own balance, often in several currencies. Give it its own account in the ledger, with fees and conversions posted as they happen. The common failure without integration is a PayPal balance that never matches the books because conversion differences and small fees were never recorded.

### 3. Wise Business

**Data flow:** Wise to ERP. Account statements per currency, conversions, fees and outgoing payments. A daily import through the Wise API is normal.

Companies use Wise to hold EUR, USD or GBP and pay foreign suppliers. The ERP needs each currency balance as its own bank account and the conversion rate actually applied, not a rate typed in later. If you trade across currencies, our guide to [multi-currency ERP](https://inovexa-erp.com/blog-multi-currency-erp.html) explains how realised and unrealised FX gains should be booked.

### 4. Open-banking bank feeds (or Plaid)

**Data flow:** Bank to ERP. Statement lines with date, amount, counterparty and reference, typically once or several times a day.

In the UK and EU, open-banking rules let regulated providers read account data with your consent. Plaid offers similar access in the US, Canada, the UK and parts of Europe. The ERP then suggests matches: the 1,200.00 credit with reference INV-2041 against invoice INV-2041. Without a feed, errors from the first week of the month are found four weeks late.

## E-commerce

### 5. Shopify

**Data flow:** Both ways. Orders, customers, refunds and payouts go to the ERP. Product data, prices and available stock go back to Shopify. Orders sync in near real time through webhooks; stock levels every few minutes.

Done properly, a Shopify order creates a sales order in the ERP, reserves stock, generates the invoice, and the Shopify Payments payout is booked net of fees to the bank clearing account. The classic failure without it is overselling: the warehouse ships the last unit to a wholesale customer while Shopify still shows three in stock.

### 6. WooCommerce

**Data flow:** Same pattern as Shopify, through the WooCommerce REST API. Orders in, stock and prices out.

WooCommerce runs on your own WordPress install, so reliability depends on your hosting and plugins. A plugin update can change order statuses or tax fields and quietly break the sync. Test after every update.

### 7. Amazon Seller Central

**Data flow:** Amazon to ERP for orders, FBA inventory and settlement reports; ERP to Amazon for stock (for merchant-fulfilled items) and sometimes prices.

The hard part is the settlement report. Amazon pays out per settlement period, usually every two weeks, after deducting referral fees, FBA fees, advertising and refunds. Post one summary journal per settlement, split by fee type, rather than matching every order. Without it, Amazon margin is a guess. Stock held in Amazon warehouses should also appear as its own location in the ERP; our [inventory management guide](https://inovexa-erp.com/blog-inventory-management-erp.html) covers why location-level stock matters.

## CRM and marketing

### 8. HubSpot

**Data flow:** HubSpot to ERP for companies, contacts and closed-won deals. ERP to HubSpot for invoice status, payment status and order history. Event-driven or every 15 to 30 minutes is typical.

When a deal moves to closed-won, the ERP creates the customer (if new) and a sales order or quote with the same line items. Without the link, sales chases customers who already paid, and finance creates duplicate customer records with slightly different spellings.

### 9. Salesforce

**Data flow:** Same direction as HubSpot. Accounts, opportunities and quotes go to the ERP; orders, invoices, credit limits and outstanding balances come back.

Salesforce orgs are often heavily customised, so field mapping takes longer than expected. Decide early which system owns the customer record. If both can edit the billing address, they will drift apart within a month.

### 10. Mailchimp

**Data flow:** Mostly ERP to Mailchimp. Customer lists, purchase history and segments such as "bought in the last 90 days" or "has not reordered". Daily is usually enough.

The ERP knows who actually buys. Sending that to Mailchimp lets you email reorder reminders to the right people instead of the whole list. Only sync contacts who opted in, and let unsubscribes flow back so nobody is re-added by the next sync.

## Productivity and communication

### 11. Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace

**Data flow:** Both ways, in small pieces. Invoices and statements sent from Outlook or Gmail, supplier emails attached to records, ERP data pulled into Excel or Google Sheets for analysis, calendar entries for deliveries or visits.

The most valuable piece is often the spreadsheet link: a live connection or scheduled export so the finance team stops copying tables by hand every Monday. If spreadsheets are still running core processes, read [ERP vs spreadsheets](https://inovexa-erp.com/blog-erp-vs-spreadsheets.html) first, because an integration will not fix a process that should not live in Excel.

### 12. Slack

**Data flow:** ERP to Slack, sometimes with actions back. Alerts and approval requests, sent as events happen.

Good uses are narrow: "Purchase order PO-3310 for 18,400 needs your approval", "Stock of SKU 2207 below reorder point", "Payment from Client X received". Posting every new order into a channel nobody reads is not.

## Documents and e-signature

### 13. DocuSign

**Data flow:** ERP to DocuSign to send a contract, quote or supplier agreement; DocuSign back to the ERP when the envelope is completed, with the signed PDF. DocuSign can notify your system by webhook as soon as signing finishes.

The signed document should attach to the customer or order record, and the status change can trigger the next step, such as releasing the order. Without it, signed contracts sit in someone's inbox and sales orders wait for a person to notice.

### 14. Dropbox or Google Drive

**Data flow:** ERP to storage for generated documents (invoices, delivery notes, payslips), storage to ERP for incoming supplier invoices dropped into a watched folder.

The ERP should remain the record; the storage is the archive. Use a consistent folder and file naming scheme, such as year / customer / invoice number, and check sharing permissions. A shared folder full of payslips is a data protection problem.

## Shipping

### 15. ShipStation

**Data flow:** ERP to ShipStation for orders ready to ship; ShipStation to ERP for tracking numbers, carrier used and actual shipping cost. Usually every few minutes or on each status change.

The shipping cost coming back matters more than people think. Without it, you know what you charged the customer for delivery but not what it cost, and margin per order is wrong.

### 16. DHL, FedEx and UPS carrier APIs

**Data flow:** ERP to carrier for shipment details, weights and customs data; carrier to ERP for labels, tracking events and rates.

Direct carrier APIs make sense when you ship mostly with one or two carriers and want to skip a middle layer. For international shipments, the ERP should send HS codes, country of origin and declared values from the product record, so customs paperwork does not get filled in by hand at the packing bench.

## HR and time

### 17. Deel (or Remote.com)

**Data flow:** Deel to ERP. Payroll and contractor payment totals per period, split by entity, cost centre and currency, usually monthly. Employee master data can go either way.

Employer-of-record and contractor platforms pay people in countries where you have no entity. The ERP needs one journal per pay run with the right cost centres, not a single lump labelled "Deel". Without that, you cannot tell what a project or department really costs.

### 18. Clockify or Toggl Track

**Data flow:** Time tracker to ERP. Time entries by person, project and task, daily or weekly. Both tools have public APIs.

For service businesses, this is the link between hours worked and money billed. Billable hours flow into project invoices; all hours flow into project costing. Without it, invoices are built from memory at month end, and unbilled hours are simply lost.

## Analytics and automation

### 19. Power BI

**Data flow:** ERP to Power BI only. Sales, margins, stock, receivables and payables, refreshed on a schedule (several times a day is common, depending on your licence).

Power BI should read from the ERP, never write to it. Agree on definitions first. If "revenue" means invoiced in one dashboard and booked orders in another, the board meeting turns into an argument about numbers.

### 20. Zapier or Make

**Data flow:** Whatever you build. Typical small flows: a web form creates a lead, a new supplier invoice email creates a draft bill, a signed contract posts a Slack message.

Good for low-volume, non-critical flows that would never justify a developer. A poor fit for the order-to-cash backbone, as the next section explains.

## ERP integrations: native connector, API, iPaaS or custom middleware

There are four common ways to connect an app to an ERP.

- **Native connector.** Built and maintained by the ERP vendor or the app vendor. Fast to set up and someone else fixes it when an API changes. The trade-off: it does what it was designed to do, and field mapping or edge cases (partial refunds, bundles, multiple warehouses) may not be configurable.
- **Direct API integration.** Your developer or partner writes code against both APIs. Full control over mapping, timing and error handling. The trade-off: you own the code, the hosting and every future API version change.
- **iPaaS (Zapier, Make, n8n).** Visual workflows with prebuilt app modules. Quick to build and easy to change. Zapier and Make are priced per task or operation, so costs rise with volume; n8n can be self-hosted, which moves the cost to running and maintaining it yourself. Error handling is thinner than in custom code, and complex flows get hard to read.
- **Custom middleware.** A dedicated integration layer (your own service or an enterprise integration platform) that sits between many systems, with queues, retries, logging and monitoring. Right for high volumes or many connected systems. The trade-off: it is a project with real build and running costs.

Use native connectors where they cover your process, the API for core flows with volume or money attached, and iPaaS for the small things. The [shift toward API-first ERP](https://inovexa-erp.com/blog-erp-news-composable-api-2026.html) has made direct API work far more practical than it was a few years ago.

## Integration checklist

Answer these before anyone writes a line of code or opens Zapier:

1. **System of record per data type.** Customers in the CRM or the ERP? Products and prices in the ERP or the shop? Write it down. Two masters for the same field means conflicts.
2. **IDs and mapping.** Store the external ID (Shopify order ID, Stripe charge ID) on the ERP record. Map tax codes, payment methods, warehouses, currencies and units of measure explicitly.
3. **Sync frequency.** Real time for stock and orders, daily for bank lines and marketing lists, per period for payroll and settlements. Faster is not always better; it costs API calls and money.
4. **Error handling and retries.** What happens when the ERP is down or a product code does not exist? Failed records should go to a queue that someone reviews, with automatic retries for temporary errors. Make each write safe to repeat so a retry does not create a duplicate invoice.
5. **Permissions and API keys.** Use a dedicated integration user with the minimum rights needed. Store keys in a secrets manager, not in a spreadsheet, and rotate them when staff leave.
6. **Monitoring.** A daily check that counts match: 214 orders in Shopify yesterday, 214 sales orders in the ERP. Alerts when a sync has not run for an hour.
7. **Ownership.** One named person or partner owns each integration, knows how it works and gets the alert when it fails.

Integration work is also one of the costs buyers most often leave out of ERP budgets. Our article on [hidden ERP costs](https://inovexa-erp.com/blog-erp-hidden-costs.html) covers how to estimate it.
